name: The Bloom Filter
statement: Test set membership with tiny space, allowing false positives but never false negatives.
statementAccent: allowing false positives but never false negatives
meaning: A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is a member of a set. Its defining trade-off is that it can produce false positives but never false negatives: a query returns either possibly in the set or definitely not in the set. If it reports that an element is absent, that is certain; if it reports that an element is present, it might be wrong, a false positive. Elements can be added to a Bloom filter but, in the standard version, cannot be removed, though a variant called a counting Bloom filter supports deletion. Internally, a Bloom filter is a bit array of some length, all bits initially zero, together with several independent hash functions. To add an element, one feeds it to each of the hash functions to obtain several positions in the bit array and sets all of those bits to one. To test membership, one hashes the element with the same functions and checks the corresponding bits: if all of them are one, the element is reported as possibly in the set; if any of them is zero, it is definitely not in the set, because adding it would have set that bit. The structure is far more space-efficient than storing the elements themselves or using a hash table, at the cost of the false-positive probability, which depends on the size of the bit array, the number of hash functions, and the number of elements inserted. It was invented by Burton Howard Bloom in 1970. Bloom filters are widely used in databases, caches, and networks.
mechanism: A Bloom filter answers set-membership queries approximately, trading a controlled chance of false positives for dramatic savings in space, and it does so with nothing more than a bit array and a handful of hash functions. The array is a fixed number of bits, all starting at zero, and the filter is equipped with several independent hash functions, each mapping any element to a position in the array. To insert an element, the filter hashes it with each function, producing several positions, and sets the bit at every one of those positions to one; different elements set overlapping patterns of bits, and the array is never reset. To query whether an element is present, the filter hashes it with the same functions and inspects the same positions: if even one of those bits is zero, the element cannot have been inserted, because insertion would have set that very bit, so the answer definitely not in the set is certain, and false negatives are impossible. If instead all the queried bits are one, the filter answers possibly in the set, but this can be a false positive, because those bits may have been set to one by the insertion of other, different elements that happened to hash to the same positions. The probability of such a false positive rises as the array fills, and depends on three quantities: the length of the bit array, the number of hash functions, and the number of elements inserted, which can be balanced to hit a target error rate with remarkably few bits per element. Because the filter only sets bits and never records which element set them, standard Bloom filters cannot support deletion, since clearing a bit might undo the record of some other element; the counting Bloom filter replaces bits with small counters to allow removal.

examples.text: Hash the element with each function and set every resulting bit in the array to one.
If any queried bit is zero, the element was never added, so absence is certain.
If all queried bits are one, the element is possibly present, but other elements may have set those bits.

whyItMatters: The Bloom filter is a small marvel of data-structure design, a way to test set membership using a tiny fraction of the space that storing the elements would require, and it is used throughout modern systems precisely because that space savings is so valuable. Its power comes from accepting a bounded, tunable chance of false positives while guaranteeing no false negatives, which fits a common pattern: a quick, cheap check that can rule things out with certainty and only occasionally raises a false alarm that a slower, exact check then resolves. This makes Bloom filters ideal for avoiding expensive work. Databases built on log-structured merge trees, such as Cassandra, HBase, and Bigtable, use Bloom filters to skip disk lookups for keys that are definitely absent, saving enormous numbers of slow reads; web caches use them, including to avoid caching one-hit-wonder URLs; and they appear in network routers, spell checkers, distributed systems, and cryptocurrency clients. In every case, a few kilobytes of bits stand in for a set that might otherwise take megabytes, and the occasional false positive costs only a redundant check. Invented by Burton Bloom in 1970, the structure remains a textbook example of how embracing a little uncertainty can buy a great deal of efficiency. As the structure that tests membership with tiny space, allowing false positives but never false negatives, the Bloom filter is a cornerstone of space-efficient computing.

working.text: start with a zeroed bit array and several independent hash functions.
hash each inserted element to several positions and set those bits to one.
report definitely not present if any queried bit is zero, otherwise possibly present.

limits: The Bloom filter is elegant but its guarantees are one-sided and conditional, and several points reward care. It can report false positives, saying an element may be present when it is not, so it must be paired with an exact check whenever a positive answer needs to be certain; only its negative answers are definite. Its false-positive rate is not fixed but rises as more elements are inserted and depends jointly on the bit-array size, the number of hash functions, and the element count, so the filter must be sized in advance for the expected load, and overfilling it degrades accuracy. A standard Bloom filter cannot delete elements, because clearing bits could corrupt the record of others; deletion requires the counting Bloom filter variant, at extra space. The filter also cannot enumerate its elements or retrieve associated values; it only answers membership. Some details reward care: it was invented by Burton Howard Bloom in 1970 in the paper Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors, and its guarantee is no false negatives, not no errors at all. So the Bloom filter robustly tests membership in tiny space, understood as a structure with certain negatives but uncertain positives, no deletion by default, and accuracy that depends on being sized for its load.
misreadings: The Bloom filter does not answer membership exactly; a positive result may be a false positive, and only negatives are certain. It does not support deletion in its standard form, nor does it store or enumerate the elements themselves. And its error rate grows as it fills, so treating a positive as definite, expecting to remove elements, or ignoring the load it was sized for, misreads it.
origin: The space-efficient probabilistic membership structure invented by Burton Howard Bloom in 1970, using a bit array and several hash functions to allow false positives but never false negatives.
